title: the yoga of Arjuna's despair
hookLine: Arjuna's body gives way, and why the Gita calls his despair a yoga.
carry: even despair is a yoga in the gita
tomorrow: what does a warrior, about to fight, say he doesn't want?

lines: CAN A SACRED TEXT LET SOMEONE FALL APART?
cards: Before a big moment a body can take over: a dry mouth, shaky hands, knees that won't hold still. One question for today: can a sacred text let someone fall apart, out loud, on the page?
The Gita's first chapter answers in Arjuna's own voice. So far he's been seen from outside. He raised his bow.
He spoke to Krishna. He looked. Then he describes himself, and the small words change to mama and me: my.

teach.b: Sanjaya sets it up: pity, kripa, took him over, and he spoke. Then Arjuna: drishtvemam svajanam krishna yuyutsum samupasthitam. Having seen my own people, Krishna, standing near, eager to fight.

teach.h: MY LIMBS SINK. MY MOUTH GOES DRY.
teach.b: Sidanti mama gatrani: my limbs sink. Mukham cha parishushyati: and my mouth goes dry.
Gandivam sramsate hastat: Gandiva, the bow, slips from my hand. He doesn't throw it. The verb belongs to the bow: it slips.
And the Gita doesn't cut him off; he speaks in full before Krishna answers. The tradition even gives this chapter a surprising name.
In the line that closes it, chapter one is called Arjuna Vishada Yoga: the yoga of Arjuna's despair. Yoga, for a breakdown.
Many teachers read that as the Gita's first lesson: the path starts where a person stops pretending to be fine.
In chapter two Arjuna says it outright, I am your student, teach me, and only then does Krishna's teaching begin. A neighbor tradition keeps words like these too.

teach.h: A PSALM: POURED OUT LIKE WATER.
teach.b: In the Psalms, kept by Jews and Christians, a voice says: "I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax."
What's shared: a sacred book that lets a body's collapse be said plainly, in the first person.

One honest difference: the Psalm is spoken to God, a prayer from inside the trouble. Arjuna speaks to Krishna, here still his charioteer and friend, and he's making a case not to fight. Krishna's reply will push back.

how: Some Hindus read the Gita in order, a chapter at a time, so Arjuna's despair, the chapter called Arjuna Vishada Yoga, is heard in full before Krishna's reply begins.

games.q: a friend reads Psalm 22 at a funeral and says it reminds them of a Gita verse. what's shared, and what's different?
o: shared: a body's collapse said plainly. different: the Psalm is prayed to God; Arjuna argues with his charioteer.
nothing is shared; one is a song and the other is a battle poem.
they're the same passage, translated from one book into the other.
games.why: both let a body's collapse be said in the first person; the Psalm is a prayer to God, and Arjuna's words are a case not to fight.

practice: Close your eyes if you like, and move your attention slowly from your feet to your hands, your mouth, your breath, naming each place silently as you reach it.
Where anything feels tight or dry or shaky, leave it be, and simply know it's there. If you pray, end with one honest line to God about where you are, the way Arjuna did.
If closing your eyes isn't comfortable, lower your gaze to the floor.

wordCard.voice: Vishada: despair, the name the tradition gives Arjuna's chapter. My limbs, my mouth, my hand: the Gita's first yoga is an honest collapse.

orig.note: Sanskrit: gandiva, Arjuna's bow; in this passage it slips from his hand.

carryVoice: Your line: even despair is a yoga in the gita. Arjuna said it all first. That's today's reading.
